speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I should like first to join with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. MacNicol) in congratulating the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald) on the ease and eloquence with which he addressed this house in his first speech here. I imagine that possibly, like myself, he is somewhat handicapped in speaking to the house by not being permitted to address it in his mother tongue.
The speech from the throne which was read at the opening of parliament contained these words:

You have been summoned at this time that opportunity may be afforded for the fullest consideration and discussion of Canada's war effort and of national problems which war has served to intensify or create.
That states very clearly the reasons for calling us here, I think. I for one believe it is highly desirable that at this time we should have a full and free discussion of Canada's war effort and related problems. Though now we have been at war for more than fourteen months there has been very little opportunity for the private member, at least the private member on this side of the house, to obtain a clear picture of what the country has done and is doing in this great emergency. Perhaps it is difficult to give a clear picture without making public information which might be helpful to the enemy. We should keep in mind, however, that too little information may be as harmful to our cause as too much.
Already, since the opening of this session, we have heard a great deal about the military preparations which the country is making to carry the war to a victorious conclusion. If we are going to wage war at all I think we should do so with all the power at our command, if for no other reason than to bring the terrible ordeal to a successful ending as quickly as possible. We should not, however, lose sight of the fact that preparation for war is not a military problem only. It is also an economic problem, a political problem and a psychological problem. If, then, we think only in terms of military preparation, whatever may be the military result we will lose the war. For us I hope that winning the war is not to be an end, but rather the means to an end. If that is the case, as I sincerely hope it is, we must keep that end continually in mind. I think that is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) must have had in mind when he said, as reported at page 61 of Hansard'.
What is necessary then to win the present conflict: It is to put on the whole armour of God, not the outward material trappings only, the helmet, the sword and the shield, necessary as they may be for purposes of defence and attack.
There is much more in the Prime Minister's peroration to the same effect, but I think I have quoted enough to show that he holds that in this struggle the use of military instruments is not enough to win the war. We must also make use of other, if more intangible, things, such as fair dealing, honour, truth, justice, equity, cooperation, the willingness to sacrifice, and many similar virtues

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
which people of good-will all through the ages have tried to get accepted as the foundations for the society of their day.
If that is what the Prime Minister meant, and I believe it is, then I am in absolute agreement with him; and because I believe as I do I am greatly disturbed about the lack of understanding and of the practice of the truths mentioned by the Prime Minister on the part of most of the people who have to do with the direction of our war industries. Since the war started we have heard a great deal of that much misunderstood word, democracy. In modern warfare the morale and temper of the workers in industry in my opinion is of equal importance to the morale of the soldiers in the army. Relations in industry between employers and workers are not good in Canada to-day, and are daily becoming worse. For this the government must accept responsibility. I think this is more particularly true of our war industries.
Let me outline briefly the position of the worker as he sees it himself. He feels that he is being exploited, that the contractors are making an undue profit out of his labour and out of the distress of the country. Moreover, he feels that he has been ignored by the government. He feels that the government is working hand in hand with the employers to prevent his having a say as to the terms upon which he will sell his labour. He is losing faith in the sincerity of those who are governing this country, not only those in the government itself but the people who have great influence upon the government. Steps should be taken at once to remedy this condition if we are not to have unrest very shortly which will reach greater proportions than the unrest at the end of the last war.
I should like to refer for a moment to my own city of Vancouver. Perhaps this matter is a small one, but it is just one of a number of small things which are likely to increase and make for a bad situation. The Boeing aeroplane company have a plant in Vancouver which has had, and I believe still has, government contracts for the manufacture of aeroplanes and aeroplane parts. According to a recent press statement the government has under consideration the construction of another new aeroplane plant near the city and yet, a few weeks ago about 150 men were laid off at the Boeing plant; the reason given for the lay-off being lack of material. But the men who were laid off are not satisfied that that was the real reason. As a basis for their doubt in the matter they point out that shortly before they were laid off a considerable number of new men had been engaged. They point out that although there has been considerable talk of a scarcity of skilled labour, the employees laid off by the Boeing plant were skilled men who had been in the employ of the company for a long time, some of them for many years.
The men are also suspicious because among those laid off are some of the officers of their union. They inform me that no effort has been made by the company to observe the regulations issued by the government last January as to labour conditions applicable to contracts awarded in western Canada for aircraft manufacture and overhaul. These regulations stipulate that the ratio of apprentices -between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one years to trade journeymen shall be five journeymen to one apprentice. These regulations were applicable to a number of trades, but I am informed that, after the lay-off at the Boeing plant, in the machine shop there were one apprentice and one journeyman left on the night shift, two journeymen and one apprentice on the afternoon shift and on the evening shift, three journeymen and one apprentice. In the metal shop, where there was supposed to be not more than one apprentice to five journeymen, there were left three apprentices and three journeymen.
I am told that an analysis of the capacities of the men laid off showed that in most instances, if not in all, it was production workers, journeymen and specialists, whose labour was dispensed with. I am not arguing that changes in the regulations should not be made if conditions warrant, but it seems to me that when such changes are made they should be made according to the rule laid down by the order in council P.C. 2685, passed last June, which provides that such changes shall be made only after consultation with representatives of the employers and of the employees. I submit that employers should be given to understand that war contracts are not the result of their personal initiative and enterprise. They should be told that the people of Canada pay for these contracts; that these contracts are the result of the determination of the people of this country to destroy Hitlerism, but that in doing so we are not going to allow embryo Hitlers to develop among us.
Further with regard to the growing discontent among the working people I should like to remind the house that at the last session I directed attention to the lack of labour representation on the various war boards. At this time I should like to advise the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) again that if he wants the people of this country to continue in the faith that this is a war to destroy Hitlerism and to save democ-
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

racy he had better review without delay some of the appointments which have been made to these boards since the war began. I do not refer to the armed forces; I refer to the personnel of many of the war boards, particularly to the appointments made to the former munitions and supply board, most of whom have since been taken into the Department of Munitions and Supply. I want to say most emphatically that at this moment there are men in influential positions who should be retired quickly. I am not denying that they may know a great deal about business and industry, but they know nothing at all about democracy. Because they know nothing about democracy there is likely to be trouble in this country before very long. It may be better to have a little dislocation now than a great upheaval later on.
Last June the government issued an order in council, the one to which I referred a moment ago, which set out the principles and conditions which should govern the conduct of employers and workers during the war. In that order in council the government gave its approval to collective bargaining. Collective bargaining presupposes union recognition by the employer; indeed, collective bargaining is impossible without union recognition. I do not know whether this order in council has had any effect upon the attitude of employers toward collective bargaining, but from what I hear and from the evidence I have, I doubt it. I believe that most employers, with a few honourable exceptions, treat it with contempt.
I drew attention last session to a conciliation board which had been set up to investigate a dispute between local 240, Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers' Union at Kirkland Lake, and Teck-Hughes Gold Mines, Limited. As I remember the case now, there were three points in dispute-wage increases, union recognition, and the reinstatement of a number of employees, 47 in number, who had been discharged for alleged union activities. The members of the board were Mr. Justice Martin of Saskatchewan, Mr. J. L. Cohen, a lawyer of Toronto, and Mr. G. C. Bateman, who I understand is at the moment economic adviser to the Minister of Munitions and Supply. Mr. Justice Martin and Mr. Cohen, in a majority report, recommended that the discharged men be taken back before any new men were hired, and that lay-offs and rehiring in future be according to seniority. They also found in favour of union recognition, but found against an increase in wages for the time being. But Mr. Bateman, economic adviser to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, found against all the claims of

the men, including union recognition. However, the men agreed to accept the award shortly after it was made. Forty-four days after the men had agreed to accept the award, just a month and a half afterwards, Teck-Hughes Gold Mines, Limited, in a letter signed by the president himself, advised the Department of Labour in these words:
I beg to inform you that at a recent meeting of our board of directors it was decided that the recommendations made by the board of conciliation and investigation wrould not be accepted by this company.
Order in council P.C. 26S5, which I have already mentioned, reads, in clause 7:
That employees, through the officers of their trade union or through other representatives chosen by them, should be free to negotiate with employers or the representatives of employers' associations concerning rates of pay, hours of labour and other working conditions with a view to the conclusion of a collective agreement.
With an experience, Mr. Speaker, of over thirty years in the trade union movement, and at least that length of time studying the relations between employer and worker, I am convinced that there is no other way under heaven in which there can be peace and democracy in industry except by collective agreements between employers and employees.
I have quoted this clause from the order in council because many trade unions in their innocence thought this order in council was operative, that it had some legal sanction behind it, like the order in council, for instance, which declares areas around certain industrial plants " protected areas," or like the order in council which, without any notice or consultation, and in contravention of the government's own declared policy, abrogated the Fair Wage and Hours of Labour Act of 1935 in certain works.
The workers are usually simple people. By that I mean they are not accustomed to the subtleties found in high places. Words mean to them just what the words seem to mean, and they accept them at their face value. The workers did not know that the order in council which the government passed in June last was merely window dressing and was accepted by the government as being just that. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) I imagine would call it " eye-wash," but many of the workers have another word for it, which, if I were to use it, would be considered unparliamentary and I should have to withdraw it. It is a compound word made up of the male of the bovine species and a certain kind of fertilizer.
All the nazi-minded people are not in Germany. Many of them can be found at

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
the head of Canadian industries. I am afraid that a few can be found around the Department of Munitions and Supply.
We have, I understand, a bureau of public information. At least I get through the mail a weekly budget of information after most of it is a week old. For obvious reasons- because of their age, I presume-these budgets of information do not carry any date. I have in my hand at the moment one that came not so very long ago from the Canadian office, but which seems to have originated in the British ministry of information. Here is the heading, " Nazis Crush Belgian Trade Unionism." Then follows a short statement by Max Buset, a member of the Belgian Labour party and at one time a Labour member of the Belgian parliament. I shall quote only two or three sentences from this statement. He says:
One fact emerges quite clearly from all we have heard, and that is the complete destruction of the trade union movement, such as we have known it up to May 10, when the nazi fury descended upon my unhappy country.
The first thing the nazis do when they get control anywhere is to destroy the protective institutions which the workers have built up through the years. Trade unions, labour parties, cooperative movements-all these go. But I want to ask you, Mr. Speaker, what is the difference between the philosophy of the man who crushes the Labour movement and the man who will not allow the Labour movement to come into existence, who will not allow a trade union to be born. What is the difference? No difference whatsoever. The mind of one is the mind of the other. Both minds are totalitarian in every respect; totalitarian in every sense of the word.
I had the opportunity of sitting in at some of the sessions of the recent convention of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada held at Vancouver, and I wish to say that if the temper of the delegates at that convention is any indication of the temper of the rank and file of the workers throughout the country, it is not good. At the convention strong exception was taken to the interference by the Department of Munitions and Supply, through its director of labour relations, in the matter of wages and labour conditions in war industries. It seems to me that if the facts are as stated-and the delegates to the convention were intelligent men and ought to know-then such a condition should cease at once.
I have before me a report which appeared in the Vancouver Province of the discussion on a resolution condemning the Department
of Munitions and Supply for interfering with wages and labour conditions. The subheading is:
Decisions of munitions board called prejudicial to labour.
Then it goes on:
H. B. Chase, director of labour relations for the board of munitions and supply, came in for fiery criticism Thursday when the Trades and Labour Congress adopted a resolution calling for the restoration of the single authority of the dominion Department of Labour.
One of the delegates said that-
. . . Chase had violated the entire spirit of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.
He continued:
On his visit to Vancouver last year, Chase had opposed the rate of 90 cents per hour suggested by the conciliation board which investigated the situation, and had declared he was " going to see no more shipbuilding contracts came to this coast."
That is, to the Pacific coast. It was also mentioned that no one knew upon whose recommendation Chase was put on the board. I pointed out last year that he was the only Labour representative on the munitions and supply board; yet, as I have said, at the Trades and Labour Congress, where 250 delegates were present, nobody knew by whom their representative on the board had been recommended.
The adjustment of labour-employer relations is a business in itself. It requires the understanding and experience of people who have been trained in that kind of work.
I suggest to the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) that he assert his authority in his own department. It is, perhaps, too much to expect that we shall have a proper understanding between workers and employers in our war industries so long as a man like Mr. Bateman, with his mediaeval ideas of the relations which should exist between employers and workers, is economic adviser to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe).
We should always bear in mind that we are waging a war for freedom; not freedom for the strong and powerful but freedom for the weak and defenceless. We are also fighting a war for democracy, and every victory for democracy at home will harden the will to resist nazism everywhere.
In the few minutes which are left to me, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word with regard to the defence of Canada regulations. I want to support the position taken by the acting leader of this group (Mr. Coldwell) when he spoke some days ago. I was glad also to note that last night the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) dealt
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

intelligently and comprehensively with the subject. Although it is now nearly fifteen months since these regulations were passed, by order in council, there has not been in this house any adequate discussion of them. I know that a special committee was appointed last year to review the regulations, but it met in camera, so that only the members of the committee have any knowledge of what was placed before it by those who are charged with the enforcement of the regulations, or of representations made by organizations or by individuals. I am not denying the necessity of special regulations in war time for dealing with espionage, sabotage or other activities intended to impede our war effort. But surely it is possible to protect the state and do it in such a way that reasonable men will be satisfied that injustice is not being done to innocent persons. That is a most important thing-that the public mind shall be satisfied that these regulations are so enforced that innocent people are not punished. During the closing days of the last session I brought to the attention of parliament the phase of the regulations to which I am now referring. I pointed out at that time that a number of men who held positions of responsibility in trade union organizations had been interned without the fact having been made public and without having been given any adequate opportunity of meeting the charges against them. Counsel for some of the internees have found the two review committees established under regulation 22 to be almost entirely valueless. I have under my hand a statement of two counsel describing the procedure followed by the review committee. According to the statement, the judge comprising the committee has before him the departmental file, the contents of which are not disclosed to the internee or to his counsel. The judge then proceeds to interrogate the internee, who has no knowledge of the nature of the evidence against him or of the facts on which the evidence is based. Surely this is a most undemocratic and improper review procedure. I am quite willing ito agree that in the nature of the case it may not be possible to confront the accused with the witnesses, and that it may also be necessary to hold the review in private. But precisely because the ordinary court procedure of examining and cross-examining witnesses may not be feasible, it is doubly important to take every precaution against error and injustice.
I therefore suggest that two amendments to regulation 22 must immediately be made. First, the review committee should be enlarged, to consist of at least three persons, since in the nature of the case the committee must act

as jury as well as judge. Second, the internee and his counsel should be provided with a full statement of the evidence and the facts alleged, in order that they may be in a position to meet them and to establish if possible the innocence of the accused.
I do not want what I am saying to be taken as unfriendly criticism of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I am quite willing to admit that his position is not an easy one. On the one hand, he is charged with protecting the safety of the state against the actions of subversive individuals-persons who in many instances give their first loyalty to other governments; on the other hand, he is entrusted with safeguarding the life and liberty of every Canadian citizen until he is proved guilty of some crime or action inimical to the welfare of the country. In time of war this is not an easy task.
At the time of the invasion of the low countries and of the Scandinavian countries when the hue and cry went up against fifth columnists, I received many resolutions and telegrams asking that this and that authority be set up to deal with subversive activities. In all cases I refused to give my approval to any such thing. I stated publicly at that time that there was no man in Canada to-day, likely to fill the office of Minister of Justice, whom I would rather have in that office than the present minister. I had hoped that his record of opposition to such undemocratic legislation as section 98 would guarantee that the regulations themselves would be liberalized and would be applied with care, but this hope' has not been fulfilled. The internment of trade union officials, the arrest and prosecution of people who say things in private conversation or under the influence of liquor, the use of the regulations for the purpose of arresting people who do peaceful picketing, and the general interference with freedom of speech and association constitute in my opinion as serious a threat to democracy in Canada as the country has ever seen. The least that the minister and the government can do is to provide a proper review procedure for those interned.
I was sorry that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) did not see fit to be more explicit as to the peace aims of the government. He said that if nazi Germany were not defeated, there would be little of freedom, truth and justice left in the world. I admit at once the truth of that statement, but it does not follow that if Germany is defeated, freedom, truth and justice will automatically flourish. We fought for freedom, truth and justice in the last war; millions of young men died in the belief that they were fighting for

The Address-Mr. Little
these things; but we did not get them. After the last war the struggle for wealth and power in this country went on with unabated fierceness, and we have had ever since wealth and poverty, want and abundance, mansion and hovel side by side, even in more glaring contradiction than before 1914-18.
Just as a closing word I would say that in our fight to destroy Hitlerism we must remember those basic things for which we are actually fighting. We must demonstrate, not by words, but by action, that, as J. B. Priestley said a few days ago, " democracy is a creative principle," and that we believe in it. If we are going to win this war we must begin now to break the power which enables a relatively few to appropriate to themselves the value of the labour of our people. Unless we do this we shall lose the war, whatever the result of military operations may be.

I had not intended to speak at this time, but in view of the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), I felt it my duty to set him right on some statements he made. In the first place, I wonder whether the hon. member is in favour of law and order. He states that in Kirkland Lake there are 250 men in uniform, carrying guns and so forth. That is not exactly true. There are 100. In the next place, he said that no one in that town knows what these men are there for. If he had taken proper steps to find out from people who are in a position to inform him, he would have been able to ascertain what these men are there for. They are volunteers who have freely offered to assist the local municipal police in keeping law and order in that town. Every one of them is a citizen of the town and is as good a Canadian citizen as anyone in this house. Some of them are working men; some are doctors; others are clerks, merchants and so on. I am very much displeased at the statements the hon. member has made with regard to these men. He says also that they look like the storm troopers of Hitler. I have never seen Hitler's storm troopers and do not know what they look like, but I may tell the hon. gentleman that if they look anything like these men they are a good looking bunch.
I consider it most unfair for a man to go into a district such as mine, or into any other part of the dominion, and to pick up statements here and there to suit himself, without taking the trouble to get authentic information from the proper source. As I said before, if he had gone to the reeve of the town or to the provincial police or to any of the men in the organization, he would have been correctly informed.
I should like to tell my hon. friend that at least 1,700 have enlisted from Kirkland Lake and district, and if that is not evidence of loyalty from a small town in that section of Canada I do not know what is. I have lived in the township of Teck for twenty-seven years; I know every man on that organization; I could name every one of them by their first names. I believe that the hon. gentleman should retract what he said and let the public know that he was misinformed. I do not know who gave him the information, but I can tell him the individual who gave it did not know what he was talking about.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present session of parliament was called principally in order that we might hear of the efforts of the government in connection with our war activities since parliament adjourned last August, and also hear representations regarding other activities as well. Personally I believe it to be the duty of all hon. members, whether on the opposition side or on the government side of the house, to bring to the attention of the government such matters as they consider it advisable and necessary to mention, because I believe that such matters, so long as they are not of a carping or personal nature, will be welcomed by the government, who during these strenuous days of trial must look to the elected representatives of the people for help and guidance.
It is my opinion that the people of Canada are well satisfied both with the efforts of the government and with the government itself. I challenge anyone to name a better qualified personnel than that forming Canada's present war cabinet. It may well be that the opposition do not entirely agree with that statement, but I am confident that the majority of the people of Canada will agree with it, just as I am confident that they have all faith in the integrity and ability of these men. What is most interesting, as well as extremely laudable, is the fact that from the beginning of this war up to the present time there has not been the slightest breath of scandal or suspicion of profiteering.
The other day, Mr. Speaker, you gave a ruling with regard to the reading of speeches, and for a moment I should like to refer to that matter. First I should like to compliment you upon the ruling you gave, but at the same time I should like to sympathize with you in your work of carrying it out. I quite
The Address-Mr. Reid

realize the task ahead of you; but I am confident that if it is carried out in a manner fair to all, you will have the support of all hon. members both in spirit and in deed.
There are differences of opinion with regard to the reading of speeches. I know there are those who hold the view that it might be better if speeches were read, and again there are those who do not believe that speeches should be read at all. My view is that if the practice of some hon. members reading their speeches is permitted to continue we might very well have in this parliament what in bygone days was the practice in the parliament of Great Britain; that is, we might have writers and others making a living by writing speeches for members of parliament. In that event we would have to listen to the views of writers and others outside this parliament who are not responsible to the people, such as the members of the house are. There is that danger, and I compliment you, Mr. Speaker, upon your decision, which I have no doubt will be impartially enforced in l'egard to all hon. members.
So far, as we all realize, the present conflict has been of a highly specialized mechanical nature, with the ingenuity of man having been turned to the production and use of fearful and scientific weapons. I believe, however, that Canada has overlooked up to the present, and is still overlooking, a powerful weapon which could and should be used in this war. I refer to the power of the radio. For some considerable time Germany has been using the radio in such a manner that it has become known as Hitler's secret weapon. At present Germany broadcasts day and night in twenty different languages, sending out propaganda-a great deal of it, if not all, lying propaganda-designed not only to create confusion in the minds of those who hear it but also to foster in the minds of those people sentiments hostile to Great Britain and her allies and favourable to Germany herself.
I believe Canada should commence immediately the construction of a high-powered shortwave broadcasting station so that speeches might be sent from this country to any part of the world it might be thought desirable. A short time ago the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) made a splendid speech over the air to the people of France. That speech, however, which I feel sure was of inestimable value and benefit not only to the people of that distressed but heroic country but also to the people of Great Britain, did not go direct from Canada to France as it should have done; it had to be relayed by way of the British Broadcasting Corporation facilities.

I am going to ask the government to give serious consideration to the erection of such a high-powered shortwave radio station, to which should be attached a foreign languages bureau. German propaganda is going out over the air not only to European countries but particularly now to the people of the United States and South America. Yet Canada is sitting idly by, doing nothing whatever to counteract that dangerous propaganda which is intended by Hitler to react against Great Britain and even ourselves. To illustrate my point I should like to cite one recent instance, the speech of United States ambassador Joseph P. Kennedy, in which- presumably speaking off the record, although some of us doubt it very much-he criticized Great Britain and gave it as his opinion that democracy in that country was finished. Not only was that speech broadcast throughout the United States and Canada by means of the press; it was immediately picked up by Germany and broadcast over the air to the United States, Canada and other countries as well, solely for the purpose of creating confusion in the minds of the people and bringing about an unfavourable reaction towards Great Britain. In my opinion Canada could render a valuable service by explaining to the people of this entire continent both north and south just what we are really fighting for and pointing out what it would mean if it is made possible for Hitler to win.
If I had anything to do with such a shortwave station I would not have these broadcasts made by certain professors from some of our colleges, and there are others I could mention. I would choose practical men, men of understanding and ability. At the moment I have in mind two outstanding men in this country who could render great service in this manner; I have in mind the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the right hon. Minister of Justice. If the services of the Minister of Justice could be utilized to speak in French to the French people, and those of the Prime Minister to speak to the people of the United States and, in fact, the entire American continent, both of these estimable gentlemen would render a wonderful service to Great Britain and to France. Great Britain is endeavouring to the best of its ability to circumvent the propaganda emanating from Germany and directed toward the people of this continent.
There is a further point in connection with the establishment in Canada of a shortwave radio station. As everyone knows, we have lost for the present all our markets on the continent of Europe and no none can tell what the outcome of this war will be or when we shall again have markets on that

The Address-Mr. Reid
continent. Therefore, we have been turning our eyes to South America. It is true we have been doing what we can in connection with sending trade commissioners, but had we a shortwave radio station we could aid these commissioners by broadcasts in the languages of the South American countries. A shortwave station would bring other countries closer to us and would enable us to be better understood by their peoples.
I should now like to deal with a matter having to do with enlisted men. I refer particularly to the dismissals or discharges which have taken place of men who enlisted in good faith after being medically examined and declared to be A 1. Many of these men left lucrative positions. They were examined by doctors; some, if not all, were X-rayed, and were accepted by the army as being physically fit. Later on, after a subsequent examination, some were discharged from the army and they now find themselves without jobs or money. I ask the government and the minister to take note of this serious condition. I am not speaking of the odd case; these discharges have been so numerous that to me they indicate that something is wrong with our system of medical examinations.
It was understood that there would be no haste in examining men who offered themselves for enlistment. During the last war there was a cry for men, but such has not been the situation in this war. I urge the government to grant to these men who have been discharged as physically unfit, leave of absence for a reasonable length of time, in order that they may become reestablished. At the same time I would call up on the carpet some of the doctors who have been making these examinations. In my humble view as a layman, if some of them were making the same blunders in private life as they seem to be doing with regard to the army men, they would not be practising medicine very long. The doctors do not suffer for the mistakes made, it is the enlisted or discharged men. I speak only for that part of British Columbia which I have the honour to represent. In my constituency at least a dozen men have been so discharged and they now find themselves without positions or funds with which to keep themselves or their families.
There is another matter I should like tc bring to the attention of the government. It may seem a small matter, but as far as the mental attitude of our men is concerned these small matters sometimes mean a great deal. There would seem to be unequal treatment accorded to the members of the three different branches of the service in connection with
transportation. On my way to Ottawa to attend this session of parliament I saw a platoon of forty army men on the train who had left Vancouver island to go overseas. I went through to the coach to inspect the conditions under which they were travelling and found that the men had been accommodated in a colonist car without any mattresses or bedding of any kind. One must be fair about it and say that the men were not kicking very strenuously.
The officers in charge, however, wanted to know why their men should be singled out for that kind of treatment when men belonging to the air force and the navy were accommodated in tourist cars and provided with beds. This may seem a small matter, but in my opinion we have not paid as much attention as we should in this war to psychology. All our efforts have been directed to material things. The enemy, however, is thinking of these small matters. It may be interesting to the house to know that prior to the fall of Dunkirk, Hitler gave orders that when men who belonged to Scottish regiments were captured they should be treated somewhat better than those who belonged to English regiments. He did not do this because he had any love for the men of the Scottish regiments-he had reason to feel otherwise-he did it for the simple purpose of sowing dissent among the British troops. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is not in the chamber at present, but I would ask him to see that the men who come under his department receive the same treatment as the men of the air force and the navy with regard to transportation.
The matter of free transportation has been mentioned, and my views accord with those of many other hon. members. It has been said that it would not be possible to grant free transportation to all. There is, however, one service which I think should be singled out for special treatment. I refer to the boys and seamen who may have been at sea for months and months on end, not coming near to land for weeks, let alone being able to go home. I was glad to hear the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald) say that consideration will be given to this class of the service.
Whilst I have every confidence that the government is doing everything possible in connection with our war effort. I am of opinion that many of our cabinet ministers are overworked. Some of them have far too many responsibilities to give attention to all matters which should receive attention. Not that I have heard any one of them complain,
The Address-Mr. Reid

but our war effort is getting so great that even members of parliament find it difficult to know all the boards which have been set up or even to find their telephone numbers. We are getting into a maze of boards. I would remind the government that the only voice the people of this country have is that of their elected representatives, and I ask the government to see that the elected representatives do not become the "forgotten men" of this war. While it may not be the fault of any single member of the government, all kinds of boards have been set up and it might very well happen that at the conclusion of this war some of these boards will be left in charge of important Canadian industries. I view with some alarm this tendency and deem it my duty to draw it to the attention of the government.
I have one other criticism to offer with regard to our war industries. The new factories which have been set up so far have been, generally speaking, centralized in two provinces. I feel that is a most unwise policy, both nationally and for the safety of the nation. WTho is there in this house who would dare to say that this country will never be invaded? Nay, I will go further and say that there is a possible danger of invasion. If that is so, are we then going to continue the policy of grouping Ontario and Quebec with all the major industries engaged in our war activities? I say to the government that this is an unwise policy from the point of view of the safety of the nation, and it is just as unwise as a matter of national economics.
I heaird one member of the house speak this session about the farmers in his community who, he stated, were closing up their farms because of lack of help. The help was going into war industries at more remunerative wages. That was most interesting to those of us who come from British Columbia because there, for a very different reason, we find farmers closing up their farms or, in other instances, hanging on to them precariously. The farmers in British Columbia are faced with an abundance of produce in their cellars and bams, and at the same time witness large quantities of farm products from across the line brought in by the use of Canadian funds and sold at lower prices. Our farmers see this produce coming in and passing by their doors while their own produce lies at home without a market. I mentioned this matter in my last speech, Mr. Speaker, and I repeat it now, and make the further assertion that if the industrial plants of this country are to continue to receive high protection, so should the farmers.

Before passing from that, I am going to make one further suggestion to the government, and that is with regard to overtime being worked in our war factories at the present time. So long as there is help available and an abundance of it, both skilled and especially unskilled, as there is in British Columbia, no overtime should be allowed. It is not good for the worker himself and it is certainly most unjust to the unemployed.
We have been wondering about the enthusiasm of the people in this war. We have witnessed the splendid spirit which has been exhibited by the British people, and while that spirit is indeed splendid, it is noteworthy that almost everyone in Great Britain who has been able to do any work has been employed in war efforts in one capacity or another. But in this country we have people both able and willing still -wondering what it is all about. I would ask the government to take note of the surplus labour we have in some of the provinces and see if something cannot be done about the matter.
A short time ago we heard a wonderful speech by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).

The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), in his speech the other evening, gave it as his opinion that the people of Canada are not taking this war as seriously as he thinks they should. I am rather inclined to that view, and I am frank in saying I cannot give any reason why it is so, because, as every hon. member and all other people in Canada know, conditions are serious indeed. But if such a state of mind does prevail, I believe it is the duty of this parliament to investigate and, if possible remedy it, for we must not let our war efforts or enthusiasm lag. Enthusiasm should be maintained from one end of Canada to the other until we are victorious.
People ask about conditions after the war; and this afternoon one hon. member inquired as to Canada's peace aims. While it is important that we give some thought to the aftermath of the war, all our thoughts and energies must now be directed to the present conflict, to assure that first of all Hitler and his forces shall be defeated. We are not only fighting for democracy, at the present time we are fighting for our very lives, and that is all-important. He would be a bold or wise man who to-day would attempt to predict what will come after this conflict. But, knowing the weaknesses of our own system in the past, and realizing the sorrow and suffering which some of those weaknesses imposed upon many of our citizens, I pray that our fight will be on behalf not of yesterday, but of a to-morrow, and that it will lead to the remedying of those conditions and the bringing about of a more lasting peace and happiness in the lives of untold millions of people.

Mr. Speaker, I am in agreement with many of the ideas expressed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid) who has preceded me, and particularly with the concluding words of his address, that while the expression of our peace aims should be kept before us, at this time our duty as a parliament is to do our best to ensure that first things shall come first, and that this empire shall be victorious.
Our main purpose in meeting in this short session is to hear the reports of the various ministers of the crown. As I listened to the comprehensive report of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) I was thrilled, as other hon. members must have been, at the magnificent record of the Royal Canadian Air Force. Coming as I do from Saskatchewan, it will be understood what pride I have in the fact that the commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas, Squadron Leader McNab, is a native of my own province. During the eloquent address to-day of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), in which he told of the vigilance of the Royal Navy and also of our Canadian fleet in protecting our shores and in guarding our convoys, I thought of those young men from the prairies in the Canadian fleet who had never before gone down to the sea in ships, and many of whom until the outbreak of this war had never seen the sea. The record of our air force, the courage and the initiative of our navy, and, above all, the heroic resistance of Britain during the last months, have revived and revitalized our empire.
Someone has said, "Who dies if England live?" I paraphrase those words this evening and say, "Who lives if England die?" The attitude of this empire was epitomized the other day in the words-the immortal words- of Captain Fogarty Fegen of the Jervis Bay, "We are closing in closer to the enemy." Faced as he was with overwhelming odds, he went into action, counting not the cost, and in death he saved the lives of others. Parliament is convened at this time to assure the Canadian people that Canada is closing in on the enemy, by a redoubled and ever-increasing contribution to the empire's waT effort. To-day, in consequence particularly of the resistance of the people of London, predictions are freely made of an offensive shortly to come. All of us in this parliament, irrespective of political faith, are agreed that there must be no apathy and that the war effort of this nation shall be relentlessly pursued. That is why we are here-to contribute our individual share to the end that there shall be an ever-widening effort on the part of Canada.

We of the opposition have, as I conceive it, a duty to perform. The last speaker stated and I agree with him, that it is not for us to indulge in carping criticism. It is our duty fearlessly to place our views before this parliament and this country. It is not for us to be overwhelmed by the government's superiority in numbers. If we indulge in unfair criticism, ours is an improper part. In this war, party considerations and prospects should be forgotten in a common endeavour to secure the highest and utmost degree of aid to the empire. In the United Kingdom there is active cooperation by all political parties, with the one reservation that individual members have reserved to themselves the right to criticize. But they cooperate. The Churchills, the Beaverbrooks and the Bevins, irreconcilable in many major matters in time of peace, are united in the hour of the nation's danger. We on the part of this opposition are denied active participation in the affairs of the country at this time, but we do claim the right of cooperation and the right of constructive criticism.
If I understand the vote in the last election, it amounted to this. The people of Canada wanted the party system of government to continue, but they did not want, nor did. they vote for, partisanship in the conduct of this war. Democracy can function only when an opposition is prepared fearlessly to spur on the government where it lacks and lags and at the same time to cooperate where it succeeds.
Lord Tweedsmuir, in his book, "Memory Hold-The-Door," has set out that view of democracy in these words:
Democracy-the essential thing as distinguished from this or that democratic government-was primarily an attitude of mind, a spiritual testament and not an economic structure or a political machine. The testament involved certain basic beliefs-that the personality was sacrosanct, which was the meaning of liberty; that policy should be settled by free discussions; that normally a minority should be ready to yield to a majority which in turn should respect a minority's sacred things.
We on this side of the house, in the interests of an ever-widening war effort, again plead with the government of the day to give us a secret session of parliament, not in order that we may be able to ascertain matters that may be of assistance to the enemy but in ord'er to enable us to ask questions and make suggestions that cannot be submitted in this house without danger of benefiting the enemy.
The spirit in which I approach my responsibilities as a member is this, to offer fair criticism, because it must never be forgotten that during the days of 1914-18 in this house, owing

The Address-Mr. Diejenbaker
to the criticism of members of the opposition, many millions of dollars were saved Canada in the matter of contracts; and in Great Britain, in consequence of criticism, at first ridiculed and later accepted by the government, the shell shortage which at one time threatened to bring down the empire was ultimately remedied.
There are many who say that democratic rights are being lost to-day, but with that view I do not agree. Some of these rights are being suspended on account of the greater need of national safety. Freedom of speech is one of these rights; it is of the essence of democracy. I admit, however, that in time of war there must be a pronounced degree of censorship. In what way have the people of Canada an opportunity of questioning the administration? If all members on the government side were to follow the example of the last speaker, the government would realize the attitude of the country. To-day the press of the country is in many instances subject to -too censorious a censorship. Have the Canadian people an opportunity to express their views over the radio?
The last speaker mentioned the propagandist value of the radio. What about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? It is a public body, a creation of parliament. Is it tending to become the creature of this government? Two weeks ago there appeared in Toronto Saturday Night an article entitled, "It is your two and a half bucks." In that article there are set forth in detail certain principles governing the broadcasting -corporation, one of which may be summarized thus: that anyone may use the radio in this country so long as he complies with the law, subject to this proviso, that he endangers himself and also the particular station over which he speaks if he indulges in anything of a nature that might undermine the war effort of the dominion. In that article by "Politicus" these words appear:
Instead of leaving that section alone as the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to-day, plus the provisions of the defence of Canada regulations, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has put responsible groups of parliament on.the banned list. And without a public announcement to those parties.
The people of Canada have a right to know whether that statement is correct. They have a right to know whether a ban has been placed on political parties. If it has, by whose authority was it imposed? In my opinion it is the negation of democracy.
We of the opposition can make ourselves heard only over the radio. If that right or privilege, the right of free and untrammelled discusion of public affairs, with a view 14873-15
to the creation of public opinion, has been denied to us, the essence of democracy has been destroyed. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) is not in his seat at the moment, but I suggest that immediately there be instituted an investigation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; for, if the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has become a party vehicle, parliament and the country should know -the facts. Why has that investigation been refused by the Minister of Munitions and Supply? Has the day come in this dominion when a publicly owned corporation may become a vehicle for the dissemination of information tinged with partisan bias and yet be above examination by a parliamentary committee?
We have not the numbers on this side of the house to enforce our demand for the setting up of a committee to investigate the matter of radio, but I am asking members on the government side of the house: Will you not support us in our stand that such an investigation take place?
There is one phase of help that we might give to this empire that has not yet been dealt with except by the last speaker. As I apprehend it, this parliament should be concerned with -the building up of morale in the empire as well as in Canada. As the last speaker stated, the United Kingdom needs a healthy and increasing export trade to Canada. Her increasing import of war materials requires an increase in exports in order to finance it. Recently in an editorial in the Manchester Guardian the following words appear:
We can win the war only if we can pay for it by our exports after all our other resources in gold, foreign securities and services have been exhausted. Exports therefore can be counted as munitions of war.
What do we find? British exports to all parts of the world are decreasing. For last July, exports from Great Britain decreased by 22-7 per cent compared with the corresponding month in 1939. The volume of British imports increased during the same period by 11-2 per cent. Britain cannot continue her maximum war effort unless all parts of the empire increase their purchases from her. In an editorial in the Regina Leader-Post these words appear, summarizing the view I am endeavouring to place before hon. members:
Armies, navies and air fleets are vital in the winning of wars, but the " economic arm " also plays an essential if less spectacular part. Canadians are helping to win the war with the formidable aid they are giving on land, sea and in the skies, but they can also help by buying British goods on as liberal a scale as possible.

There is no denying the fact that throughout Canada to-day there is a growing feeling of resentment at the failure of the government to cut down controllable expenditures, at the fact that many appointments to high positions are being made that savour of political considerations. It may take some time. If the prices are reasonable-and I hope they are-the publication will tend to restore confidence. Concealment can only breed suspicion, and suspicion can only breed disunity. Publicity will do no harm with the vast majority of patriotic manufacturers or other suppliers of war requirements, who ask only a fair profit. But it will be an instrument of fear to the minority who would take unfair advantage of the sacrifices of this nation and empire at this time to charge monopolistic prices. I advance this argument in all sincerity, not with a view of political advantage to any party.
Look at the situation in connection with the last war loan. The response was dilatory. Why? Because on every hand people were saying, Is it possible that things are not right and that maximum benefits are not being received from the expenditure of money? Such publication would do away with that suspicion.
I suggest further that there be set up in this parliament a public accounts committee, giving it power to examine contracts, not of a year ago but up to date. There need be no political partisanship in the deliberations of such committee. Have the investigation or examination behind closed doors, if you will. You insist that there be no suggestion of partisanship. I point to the committee that met here last session, composed of members from all parties in this house. We met together for a period of more than three months, and while there may have been some shortcomings, our whole aim was to make sure that this nation should be free from subversive activities. Set up such a committee; no one need have anything to fear so long as reason and judgment prevail. Is there anything out of the way in thalt suggestion? We must keep up the morale of this 14873-l5i
nation, and we can do that by having people realize that the money they contribute and the sacrifices they make will not be dissipated.
I should like now to say a word with regard to our soldiers and sailors. We all agree that the morale of our fighting men and their dependents must be maintained. I join in the demand that these men in the service be given free transportation during their official leaves. At the same time I suggest that a regulation be passed assuring these men, who are spread all over Canada, of a minimum length of time at home. To the man on service nothing matters so much as his home. I also commend to the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) the suggestion advanced by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) that free postage be allowed on all mail to and from men in the service. That would not be costly, but it would be a tangible recognition and appreciation of their services.
Again returning to the home front I should mention the magnificent work being done by women in connection with the Red Cross and other charitable works and aids ito the soldiers. They did wonderful work in the last war and are doing wonderful work again in this war. I think they merit the highest commendation and, What is more, recognition by the government. I suggest to the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) that women be given representation in that department, in order that they may correlate and organize the work of women throughout Canada. According to recent statistics of the Department of Labour there are in Canada to-day 52,500 employable men who are still unemployed. Bearing in mind the development of industry on every hand, I believe the time will come when it will be necessary to utilize the services of women in industry to take the places of men who are on service. To-day voluntary organizations are to be found across Canada, from Vancouver and Victoria on the west coast to Halifax in the east, receiving instruction in first-aid training and home nursing, and in motor mechanics. These organizations should be recognized; and I suggest to the government that in anticipation of the need for women in industry, courses be set up at once in connection with munitions ' manufacture, aeroplane construction, motor mechanics and gas-mask manufacture. Provision might be made for the enrolment of women along the line of the army auxiliary corps in the last war, in which women were enrolled for the period of the war, not under the war department but under a government department similar to the Department of National War Services.

I shall conclude by referring to agriculture. In common with British Columbia, which was referred to by the last speaker, Saskatchewan has not benefited to any extent as a result of the development of war industries. In fairness to that province I think some of these industries should be established there. The services of many trained mechanics are not being utilized. Small machinery plants, that could turn out munitions as they did in the last war, are not being called into service. I am sure the speech from the throne will be received with deep resentment, certainly with great disappointment, all over western Canada. It contained no announcement of any policy designed to relieve the plight of the wheat farmer. Therefore I have no apology to make for supporting the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), which states:
And this house further regrets that despite the serious condition of agriculture no effective action is proposed to alleviate that condition and to ensure to the Canadian farmer a just, fair and reasonable return for his products.
I had hoped that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would have something to offer. He spoke at some length. He made a political speech, to start with; then, instead of enunciating a policy which would be of some immediate benefit to the wheat farmers he expressed a speculative hope that at the end of five years all would be well, or at least that the surplus would have disappeared. It was not a five-year plan; it was a five-year hope. The western farmer wants to know: first, is the government going to do anything to assure him of a fair, just and reasonable return for his wheat; second, is the interim payment that was promised in the election of 1940 going to be paid, and when; third, is the government going to make advances to the farmers on the wheat held in storage?	To all those questions no
answers were given, no reference was made.
Then the western farmer wants to know whether the government intends to do anything to remove the injustice suffered by him to-day in the matter of grading wheat. The farmer is paid on the basis of 70 cents a bushel for No. 1 northern wheat at Fort William, but wheat that should grade No. 1 is being graded No. 2, No. 3 and, in some instances, No. 4. Is that for the benefit of the Canadian farmer or is it for the benefit of the elevator corporations, who to-day all over western Canada are building large storage facilities which, according to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) will pay for themselves in three months. And what is more, under the arrangement entered into by the government and these companies, the cost

of these facilities will be written off as depreciation within two years.
I have one further question to ask. What is going to be done about the payment of the bonus? In my constituency a substantial crop area was destroyed by drought and hail. The farmers want to know why they do not receive the bonus in November instead of in May. How are they to carry on through the coming winter? Is there any justification for the continued postponement of the time when a decision must be made as to whether or not the bonus will be paid? Surely this parliament has the right to know that. The Minister of Agriculture did however, make one admission. On April 5, 1939, he announced in this house that a farmer could produce wheat at from 30 to 40 cents a bushel, but speaking in the house the other day he said, as reported at page 102 of Hansard:
It is generally admitted that 70 cents advance at Fort William, which nets the farmer about 50 cents a bushel, does not cover his total costs of production and therefore does not maintain him as a contented producer. If he is to receive more money, it must come from the sale price of wheat, or from the taxpayers of Canada, or from both.
Not one thing did he say as to the future, except to express a hope of what might happen five years hence. He did, however, make one statement which I hope does not represent the considered opinion of the government to which he belongs. At page 94 of Hansard the following appears:
Why should this government change its policies on agriculture? The policies are essentially Liberal. The policies were endorsed in peace-time by the farming population of Canada when proposed in 1935. The policies were put into practice for four years and endorsed in war-time no later than March 26 last.
What does that mean? Apparently he forgot the results in the Saskatoon election which was fought after the farmers of western Canada began to realize that the promises made in the last session were not being put into effect.

During the last session of parliament the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) claimed that a policy would be announced as soon as possible. He spoke in Winnipeg on September 12, 1940, and according to the Winnipeg Tribune he stated that the war committee of the cabinet, which consisted of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the	Minister of Mines and
Resources (Mr. Crerar), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and himself, had always been ready and willing to advance money against farm stored grain. If they were and are, then make the advance. I quote further from the report in the Winnipeg Tribune.
He disagreed with the claim that the current problem of western agriculture was primarily a dominion responsibility; rather it was one for the provincial governments.
What do those words signify? What is their meaning? Do they mean that the government will do no more than it has done? Do they mean that even though the farmer has wheat in storage on his farm, he will have to depend on relief assistance to carry him through until he is permitted to sell that wheat? All I can do in this regard is to raise my voice in protest against the treatment that is being accorded to the western farmer, as evidenced by the speech from the throne. This protest will be of no avail until members representing western Canada in this house rise in their places, and, irrespective of their party affiliations, demand a fair, reasonable and just return to the western farmer and an advance on the crop at present in storage on his land.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house at large is greatly appreciative of the excellence of the speeches which we have heard since the calling of parliament, especially those of the mover (Mr. Claxton) and the seconder (Mr. Jutras) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. These hon. gentlemen are of different racial extractions, but they each gave to the people of their respective races admirable advice, which, if carried out. cannot do anything but help to solidify all the people of Canada into a true spirit of Canadianism. The moderation of their speeches, the seriousness and sincerity of their remarks, the profound knowledge of their theses and the
absence of political insinuations in what they said, I think struck a true keynote for the speeches to follow. The first speaker who followed was the hon. leader of the loyal opposition (Mr. Hanson), but he departed to some extent from the keynote of the speeches of the previous speakers. His first words as reported in Hansard are:
Macdonald! What a name to conjure with. And Macdonald of Kingston! How that takes our memories back seventy-five years; yet what a difference we see. After all:
What's in a name? That which we call a rose,
By any other name would smell as sweet.
Yet one of the greatest assets of the hon. gentleman is his name.
A somewhat similar compliment could be paid to the leader of the opposition, even to the extent of the poetical tribute and annotation. As we all know, the initials of the leader of the opposition are "R.B.". R.B.l What a name to conjure with. R.B. of the loyal opposition! How those initials must take back the memories of the opposition; not so many years. We can say with the poet:
But 0 for the touch of a vanished hand, *
And the sound of a voice that is still!
R.B.! What a name! What a source of inspiration!
All through this debate thus far there has been one point upon which all members have agreed, namely, that every effort should be put forth to win the war. I am sure that this will be the keynote of all discussions from now to the end of the war. There is no dissension on that point. That thought is unanimous on all sides, and in all sections of the house. In this we are but corroborating what an eminent writer of our day has said, namely, "What democracy has to do, and what makes it possible for democracy to continue as a functioning method of government, through the process of discussion, is to find areas of agreement on essentials." But if the end to be attained is agreed upon by all groups in the house, the same cannot be said of the means to be employed in arriving at that end. Here is where there is a parting of *the ways among the various groups in the house.
We have first the group of the loyal opposition, which contends that the government's efforts since the declaration of war by Canada have not been sufficient, that more men should have been sent overseas, that more material and equipment should have been available in our military stores, that our efforts were not properly coordinated, and finally it maintains that the government has continued to "soothe the Canadian people regarding the
The Address-Mr. Blanchette

war effort of the nation, thereby creating a false sense of security when a clear-cut call to action is desperately needed."
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group criticizes the government for not having conscripted our industries, with all that that entails, immediately upon our entry into the war.
Finally the Social Credit group is critical of our war effort because the government has not had recourse to monetary reform.
The leader of the opposition stated in his speech of November 12 last, and rightly so, that it is so easy to criticize. An eminent English writer, in discussing the operation of democracy in England, says:
We pay the minority to oppose the government, to take the maximum advantage of the government's mistakes, to insist that it is ruining the country, and to flood the electorate with propaganda intended to show that the government is doing the worst possible things in the worst possible ways.
It has also been stated that a strong and free nation comes of strong and free men, and our method of government assumes that the criticism of the opposition works in the long run for the common good of all.
At this stage of the debate it might be advantageous and I think proper for all of us to follow the oft-repeated current admonition, let us face the facts, if we wish to obtain a true perspective of what this government represents and of its achievements during the present war.
First and foremost, in my humble opinion, there is no one who can speak more truly for the majority of the people of Canada than the present government-this, whether we like it or not. The groups representing the various schools of political thought in Canada have just had an opportunity of expounding their principles, theories and programmes to the supreme authority, the electorate of the country, who pronounced themselves in no uncertain manner at the last election. In other words, the Conservative party was weighed in the balance by the electorate and was found wanting. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and its programme were also scrutinized, and that group, too, has been found wanting. Finally the Social Credit group was examined by the electorate, which, as shown by the results, decided to reform the composition of the house by decimating the representatives of that group, rather than to reform the monetary policy of the country. So once again, whether we like it or not, the present government stands out as the truest form of expression of the attitude of the Canadian people.

There are groups in this house, and outside who claim to speak for the whole people of Canada or for the majority of the electorate, but by what authority is not known. In 1932, sixty per cent of the United States press opposed Roosevelt as a candidate for the presidency. In 1936, eighty per cent of the United States press again opposed him, and ninety per cent of the United States press opposed him on November 5 last, with results that we all know, thereby revealing that at times the most vociferous are out of step and tempo with the aspirations of the electorate of the country at large.
And now if I may have the liberty, Mr. Speaker,.I should like to set out in a brief and cursory way the accomplishments of this government since the declaration of war by Canada in September, 1939, even at the risk of repeating what has already been stated in the house by persons of much greater authority than I, and remembering always the state of our equipment for army, navy and air when this government assumed power in 1935. Practically nothing had been done in the previous five years in the way of expenditure on our military, naval and air forces, but to-day the total strength of the Canadian active service force is 167,417; non-permanent active militia, officers and men, 65,000; navy personnel as of November 7 last, 13,034; recruits under training each month in thirty-nine camps, at least 25,000; air force, total number of officers and men, 30,599; enlistment of air crews as of November 2 last, 6,884; or a total of 307,934.
We have to-day in commission 140 vessels, 17 corvettes, 4 mine-sweepers and 12 destroyers. Contracts for munitions, war supplies and equipment as of November 4 last, total $443,000,000; and capital expenditures for plant construction and extensions, $235,000,000.
Plans have been accepted for the manufacture of 3,000 tanks, and at the end of the first year of the Bren gun contract _ there should be three times as many guns delivered as were called for by the contract.
The establishment of the war-time prices and trade board and the foreign exchange control board is an achievement of which this government may well be proud owing to the beneficial results derived therefrom by the Canadian people.
Let us not forget, too, that the unity which we find throughout the length and breadth of Canada to-day was not a product of spontaneous generation but was brought about rather by good judgment, able leadership and far-sightedness.
Last but not least, I believe that in large measure the people of Canada and of the whole British empire are greatly appreciative of the Ogdensburg agreement of August 17

The Address-Mr. Blanchette
last. This agreement may not have been accomplished to the blare of trumpets and the beating of drums or with astronomical figures affecting our economy or the treasury, but often the greatest events in history are predicated upon simplicity, quietude and farsightedness.
Let us not lull ourselves into the belief that this accomplishment was an inspiration which came to the United States overnight, especially since it wras announced during the course of an election campaign. It was brought about through the continued amicable relations and interviews which occurred between the United States and this country under Liberal administrations. One of the greatest acts among the many outstanding to the credit and achievement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is the consummation of the Ogdensburg agreement, a magna charta in the history of democracies. It is patent to us that this is one of the effects of the friendly relations which the Prime Minister has always fostered, nurtured and developed with the great republic to the south. I do not wish to convey the impression that the advantages of this agreement are only unilateral, but I feel that it is of the greatest importance for the aim which all free countries have in view, namely the crushing of bandits and gangsters on the international highways of the world.
These are some accomplishments of the government since the declaration of war by Canada. As has been truly stated, the government does not have to defend or justify its achievements; they defend themselves. That there may have been misgivings or misjudgments here and there may be granted. But what country has not made mistakes in its transition from peace to war activities? For example, in 1937 France manufactured throughout the whole year only thirty-eight aeroplanes, while Germany was making 100 a month, or 1,200 in a year. In the eight months prior to September, 1939, there were working in the Renault arsenal shops in France only 7,000 men out of a force of
30,000	which was the regular peace-time strength; 23,000 of those artisans were doing manual labour in the army.
In January, 1940, apart from the Canadian division no one could show us a corps of troops superior to a battalion. If we take our efforts as a wrhole and visualize them as such, I believe that no one with an open mind will deny that what we have done shows a really epic effort, a thoroughly united effort. If we grant that this government may have made mistakes, where is the guarantee that the critics of the administration might not
have made miscalculations and misjudgments? If we establish a true comparison between the efforts of this government during the first fifteen months of the war and the efforts of the administration which was in power during the last war, this government stands up favourably in all its fields of effort, and the preponderance wiLl not be spurious.
I have clipped from this morning's Montreal Gazette an article headed, "Canadian war costs to date over 1914-18":
London, November 18.-Hon. Vincent Massey, Canadian High Commissioner, said in a broadcast to-night that Canada has nearly as many men under arms now as at the end of the last war, and that her war expenditures since the outbreak are greater than in the whole four years of the 1914-18 conflict.
As has often been stated in this house by responsible ministers of the crown, corroborated by persons in high command in England, our cooperation with England has been of the fullest, and I feel that the Canadian people are satisfied with the efforts of the present government. In accordance with the true spirit and essence of democracy let us all cooperate, as much as possible, not only by word but by thought and deed, in this our supreme effort in the history of Canada and the British empire.
There are other matters, referring to the agricultural interests of the country, which I should like to bring to the attention of this house before taking my seat. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is to be commended for bringing back to this country the agreement which he did. It is noted, for example, that we shall be able to sell bacon to Great Britain to the extent of $69,000,000.
