speechtext:
We shall be able to export cheese in the coming year to the volume of 112,000,000 pounds at 14-4 cents; condensed milk to the extent of some $3,750,000; frozen fish of the value of $12,100,000, and fruit and honey to the amount of some $4,500,000. It is to be hoped that by such a diversion of dairy products the butter market will be enhanced during the producing time of the year. I know that at the present time butter obtains a fair price, but unfortunately the majority of farmers got 20 cents for their butter which is now selling for 30 to 35 cents, the difference going into the hands of those who bought at the low price and stored the product for enhancement. At 20 cents a pound for butter, the farmer is receiving about 72 cents a hundred pounds for his milk which is costing him between $1.69 and $2.04 to produce, depending on the
The Address-Mr. Blanchette

size of the herd, as per data obtained during a recent survey in the county of Deux Montagnes, a survey made under the direction of Professor Toupin of l'Institut d'Oka. These conditions have been prevailing for a number of years in the butter industry, and the attention of the government is drawn to this disparity between the cost of production and the return upon same during the producing time of the year.
If the wheat grower, the apple grower, and the potato grower must receive the attention of the government in order to carry on, surely the same consideration is more necessary for the farmer who is engaged in the production of butter, which needs a farmer's attention 365 days of the year. I trust that the government will devote its most sincere consideration to this branch of the dairy industry. If I may be permitted to offer a suggestion, I would say that a reduction in the transportation cost of feed would be of great assistance to the dairy industry; or again, the providing of storage facilities, with interim government payments to the producer, would enable the butter producer to gather all the profits derived from his production, which he is not at present getting, and this with no increased cost to the consumer.
Another matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the government is heating with wood to aid our war effort. A timely editorial in this regard appeared in the Sherbrooke Daily Record in which it is stated that, where practicable, Canadian householders can achieve the dual objective of aiding in winning the war and at the same time reducing their annual expenditure for fuel by the increased use of wood for domestic heating purposes, according to information gathered by the forest products laboratories of the Department of Mines and Resources.
Each year, for domestic consumption in Canada, quite apart from industrial uses, about 3,400,000 tons of anthracite coal and about 1,800.000 tons of bituminous coal are imported. In addition, homes equipped with oil burners necessitate the importation of a considerable quantity of crude oil from which fuel is derived. Under present conditions, when every effort is being expended to conserve foreign exchange, it is important that Canada's outlay for imported fuels be reduced by drawing on her abundant resources in fuel from low grade wood. At present Canada uses approximately 10,000,000 cords of wood a year for domestic fuel. This is equal in heat value to 6.600.000 tons of anthracite. Effective heat obtained from one and one-quarter cords of good hardwood is equivalent to the heat obtained from one ton of anthracite coal.

While burning wood may entail more work and inconvenience in stoking than some other fuels, in most instances a substantial saving can be made by its use. As a measure of national economy reliance on Canadian fuel resources is important, and places within the reach of every householder a means of furthering our war effort.
I have already made this suggestion to the Department of National Defence as well as to the war supply board, in connection with the 39 training camps throughout the country, when practicable, and trust that the suggestion will be considered, as a means of conserving our foreign exchange, giving more work to our own people in lumber districts, and finally as a tangible proof that the government is carrying out the recommendations of the forest products laboratories which can be done in training centres located near lumber regions.
The war-time prices and trade board has been doing effective work in the protection of the consumer against undue profiteering, and it is to be commended for it. Undue profiteering may be derived either, on the one hand, from a price higher than a fair price, on a produced or manufactured commodity, or, on the other, by paying too low a price for the producing or manufacturing of that commodity. I believe that the war-time prices and trade board, or, if not in its jurisdiction, the departments of labour, both federal and provincial, would be well advised to be on the alert, in the way of survey and inquiry, in connection with corporations which are deriving undue benefits and profits in their handling or manufacturing of certain products and commodities. In doing so it will be rendering a great service to the producers of our basic industries, and to our labourers, both of which classes of the community need our constant attention and care.
To refer in passing to matters of provincial jurisdiction, newspapers of Quebec city, under date of November 16 last, mention a news item to the effect that the Quebec provincial government may establish a fixed price, a minimum price, on pulpwood that settlers and farmers cut on their land, and that a commission may be instituted in that regard, with powers similar to that of the dairy commission. Such a commission would render invaluable services to all concerned and I only trust that this long felt-want will become a reality in the very near future. I understand that it is a rule of thumb with the paper mills to be able to pay for pulpwood at the mill 30 per cent of the current price of newsprint as delivered at New York. This price is not being paid at present. The fact that this commission will be created speaks

The Address-Mr. Shaw
very well for the efforts of one of our former colleagues, Hon. Paul Emile Cote, who is directing, as minister, the department of lands and forests at Quebec.
Finally, in closing my remarks, may I refer to the frequent mention which is being made in the country at present of encouraging our youths in bilingualism? I have been favouring bilingualism for a number of years and would be remiss in my belief and duty if I did not profit by this occasion to state to our Canadian youth and to our educational institutions that no better preparation could be devised to develop and foster unity in the dominion and to ensure the economic success of the person so equipped. Paul Reynaud once asked, "Jeunesse, quelle France voulez-vous?" The youth of this country have already replied to this question by being in the military camps to-day. If our educational institutions are to be true to preparing our youth for the future, a fostering of bilingualism on a larger scale than has been done before cannot do otherwise than have the most beneficial results in the social, economic and national fabric of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
During
the course of the past week we have been privileged to listen to a number of addresses which I will classify as follows: First, those addresses delivered by ministers of the crown in an attempt to inform members of the house exactly what the government of the day is doing and has been doing with respect to Canada's wrar effort. Second, we have had those addresses by members of the house who are genuinely concerned about Canada's war effort and also genuinely concerned about what the outcome is going to be. Third, I believe I am quite safe in saying that there are those who are so surprised at having been elected that they cannot resist the temptation to boast about it. I believe we have just had a typical example of that.
We in this group have had reflections cast upon us from time to time, but it will be noticed that it does not stop us. One such reflection was that we have come back with reduced numbers. May I say this to the members of the house. We went to the country on a definite programme and we are still following it, whereas there are others not far away who went to the country on a definite programme which they deserted at the first opportunity. We have nothing to be ashamed of.
I was deeply interested in the addresses delivered by the ministers; most of them were quite enlightening. Much that we heard gave us courage, but there was much to depress us In dealing with the depressing aspect of 14S73-16
a certain speech, may I refer to that one delivered here on November 15 by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). This is one statement which he made:
... we still have to face the fact of a serious shortage in equipment and armament, and we shall probably have to face that fact for a good while yet in many instances.
First I wish to congratulate the minister upon being very frank. I believe that if there are shortages we the people of Canada should know about them. But I say this further, I believe that if this government five years ago had listened to the suggestions of members of this group they would not have had the same reason for stating that there are still shortages of equipment and armament. Furthermore, in connection with that same matter I say that if they were not prepared to take our advice in 1935, surely by 1937 there was ample reason for doing so, and how much better still was the reason for accepting it in September, 1939. I would make a further assertion, namely, that if the minister's statement is correct, as I have no doubt it is, there can be little good reason for there being any idle factories in this Canada of ours. There can be very little justification for there being any idle men in this country. I was appalled during the last month or two as I travelled by car through western Canada to see the great numbers of young men walking up and down the roads with packs on their backs. I made it a point to pick them up; I ascertained very early in my discussions with them where they were from and why they were out of work. There is absolutely no justification for young men walking up and down our roads in idleness at this stage of this terrific conflict.
May I refer again to the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) delivered in this house on November 14? I turn to his prognostications relative to the wheat situation. I notice his speech was literally filled with the word "assume"; assuming this and assuming that, said the minister, this will be the outcome. What did the Conservatives call it-lulling and soothing us. That, I take it, was a typical example of what they were referring to. He said in effect, assuming that the blockade is lifted, assuming that we increase consumption internally, assuming that we can sell certain quantities to the United Kingdom, assuming that we have so many years of war, and assuming that we can sell certain quantities to those countries which are not blockaded, at the end of the five-year period we shall find that we fall short by fifty million bushels of supplying the world's demand for wheat. When I heard

The Address-Mr. Shaw

the minister make those statements I almost had to classify him as the master seer, or the very personification of optimism, or an arithmetical genius. But when I observed on another page of Hansard that he referred to the fact that in the last general election our party was cut in two, which meant that half of sixteen is ten, I could place but little faith in the value of his guesses, if I may use that word, with respect to the wheat situation.
It may be a very fine thing to tell the Canadian people that there is hope in five years. I believe the Liberal party is used to things happening in five-year cycles. That is, they are either elected or defeated, and I think they cannot get the idea of elections out of their minds.
The statement of the Minister of Agriculture with respect to wheat did absolutely nothing to satisfy the farmers of western Canada who have at the present time vast surpluses of wheat, in many instances lying out without shelter in the open fields. I say, enough of these prognostications, enough of these lulling and soothing utterances, as our Conservative friends would describe them. I still think we shall have to turn to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) in order really to get an announcement with respect to the government's wheat policy.
If, Mr. Speaker, I abstain from lengthy discourse upon this occasion, it is not because I believe that parliament should abrogate its proper function, that of carrying on a debate to the fullest measure for the purpose of furthering Canada's war effort. Hon. members would be remiss in their duty if they were to leave unsaid those things which ought to be said, simply because Canada is in a state of war.
May I digress for a moment to pass one comment about the constituency which I represent. My constituents in the constituency of Red Deer are blessed in many ways. Within the bounds of that constituency we enjoy a wide diversity of activity. We have grain growing, mixed farming, dairying, mining, lumbering, manufacturing if only to a limited extent, flour milling, and the oil drilling industry even though it, too, may be only in the experimental stage. We are relatively free from the ravages of drought and insect pests, and with a few excepted areas our agricultural productivity is comparatively constant. Located in a parkland area, as we are, I assure you that much of our scenery is unsurpassed. Further, and possibly this is most important, my electors have for a good twenty years been able to
fMr. Shaw.]
reject the wooings and constant advances of all the isms, including Liberalism and Conservatism.
One would naturally assume that we have strong justification for being extremely happy. And we are. But still there are some things which have a tendency to depress us. One thing that I find depresses my constituents a great deal is the outlook for the post-war period which will come upon us just as sure as we are here. I know I may be criticized for dealing with the post-war period at this time, but I have not heard a logical argument against giving consideration to that period now. I believe that to-day is the day bo prepare for to-morrow, if we are going to be successful in meeting the conditions which will face us to-morrow.
Most hon. members who have spoken during this debate have laid a great deal of emphasis upon Canada's present objective. I realize as well as anyone does that our foremost objective is to win this war. We are fighting to win; there is no doubt about that. We have undertaken a tremendous task; there is no doubt about that either. We are making a supreme effort to protect our freedom against the dictators who would destroy it. But let us not foe deluded. We are not fighting to preserve the state of affairs which has prevailed in this country during the past decade. We are not fighting this war to preserve governments which have brought us poverty, relief, unemployment, s.qualor, hardship, the bankruptcy of agriculture and the ruin of primary industry. We are not fighting to preserve a government which will tolerate these things. We are not fighting the war to preserve a man-made set of economic rules which would work beautifully if we were living in an age of scarcity but which dismally fail to meet a condition of abundance. Those boys who left the relief lines and who dropped off box cars to enlist are not offering their lives to preserve a demoralizing existence, without hope and without prospects. I think the sooner the government of Canada realizes these facts, the more genuine will be Canada's war effort.
While referring to those boys, I believe I am quite safe in saying that although thousands of them are in uniform, willing to make the supreme sacrifice, there is in their minds an element of doubt. I will have to enlarge upon that statement in order that hon. members may know what I am getting at. I have talked with many of these young men, and they have said to me, " What is to become of us when this war is over?" To further elaborate that point I should like to read a statement appearing in the November

The Address-Mr. Shaw
16 issue of the Montreal Standard. This is just a sentence taken from a letter written by a young soldier now in a prison camp in Germany. In writing home he said:
Shall be returning home when this is all over, and settle down, I think, that is, if there are any positions open or available.
That is a good indication of what that boy is thinking about at the present time. So I say, if we are going to get the maximum effort from these boys, the very least we can do is assure them that when this war is over, they will be guaranteed economic security, such as we know this rich Canada of ours is able to provide.
We know that we must defeat the dictators, because if we do not, they will take from us freedom of speech and freedom of action. But I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we must also fight against those forces at home which would deprive us and our boys of the fruits of victory. So I say our duty to-day is twofold: first, to put every ounce of energy into the war and, second, to lay the foundation for a new society at home, a society built upon economic security which, in its new found strength, will be bound to destroy any dictatorial force which may ever face us. We must guarantee, to every boy now in uniform that when he returns he will find a way of life worthy of his noble achievements. To-day is the day to prepare, not to-morrow. We must declare openly that there shall be no starvation and no privation in a land where people are accustomed to boast about their vast surpluses of all kinds of commodities. To me, there is nothing more disgraceful and nothing with less justification than to see, in a land such as this, vast quantities of food and of materials for making clothing, and at the same time hungry and ill-clad children on every side. While we in this group have been belittled from time to time for making statements of this kind, I have yet to hear anyone, from his place in this house, or on the public platform, attempt to justify such a condition. I dare say no one would even try to do so.
I turn now to the monthly review of the Bank of Nova Scotia dated September 26, 1940, which contains these words:
One thing is clear; that the years of the last decade have in reality been years of growing warfare and cannot be regarded as a desirable standard for the future.
I commend these further words to hon. members:
A sane world has no place for millions of hungry people and great quantities of unsalable foodstuffs.
I am in absolute agreement with that states ment. When this war is over, our government must not endeavour to bring about better times simply by trying to stimulate production, as we have done in the past. That has been one great weakness of governments in days gone by; they have tried to gear up production to even greater speed in order to meet every little ill that has cropped up throughout the country. I say, and it has been said here time and again, that when this war is over, the problem we shall face will not be that of stimulating production; it will be that of distributing the abundance which we shall still have here even if this war lasts ten years
I should now like to quote just two or three paragraphs from an editorial headed, "After the War is Over," appearing in the Globe and Mail of August 9, 1940:
The problem of this century is one of distribution. The old problem of production to meet the needs and demands of the people has been solved.
When next the dominion parliament meets, it should begin to consider ways and means of providing change-over from a war-time economy to a peace-time one, bearing in mind that want shall not be necessary, and that unemployment shall not be justified on the grounds that there is no work to do-it can be explained only by the fact that we have not discovered yet how to employ labour to advantage.
A nation never goes bankrupt in the sense that it is helpless to provide for itself and its people. It can only go bankrupt according to certain financial standards which, because of the very fact that they show it as bankrupt, prove nothing but their own incompetence to reflect reality. No nation is ever bankrupt so long as it has tilled acres, uncut lumber, untapped mineral zones and so great an establishment of plant and equiment that it can produce a volume and variety of goods and services many times greater than its population can profitably utilize at the prevailing standard of life.
We are a rich people. We shall be even richer after the war. But we must begin to consider how we can best reorient our economy so that our latent capacity to produce wealth will be utilized fully and the resulting output equitably distributed.
I sajr, and I believe I am correct in saying, that the Toronto Globe and Mail is an orthodox publication. If that is true, then it would appear that even the orthodox thinkers are waking up. When I went before the people during the last general election I stated that the one thing I would press for would be the setting up of a house committee to deal with post-war problems. I was greatly pleased when I noticed in the speech from the throne of last spring the following statement:
... it is desirable, as far as may be possible, to plan for the days that will follow the cessation of hostilities.
I was pleased further to notice that on the Votes and Proceedings of the same date
The Address-Mr. Shaw

was a notice of a resolution under the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to set up a select committee of the house for the purpose of dealing with this matter. 1 was, however, chagrined when on June 18, as recorded on page 864 of Hansard, the Prime Minister saw fit to withdraw his resolution. When I returned to my constituency after the adjournment, my constituents questioned me about the attitude of the government.- toward setting up a committee, and I had no alternative than to tell them the truth. They were greatly depressed when they learned of the withdrawal of this resolution by the Prime Minister. When the Prime Minister was speaking on that occasion he stated that if it were considered advisable at a later date again to introduce the resolution, it would be done. Apparently it was not considered advisable to do that during the time the house was in session.
About the time that the house reconvened I noticed that the government had set up a subcommittee of the cabinet, made up largely of civil servants, which was to act as an advisory committee to the government in dealing with post-war problems. The thought came to me: WThy was it deemed advisable to set up a committee made up largely of civil servants instead of a committee made up of the elected representatives of the people? No matter what other committees have been set up for the purpose of studying post-war problems, I say in all sincerity that a house committee should be set up forthwith. May I say to this committee, or to any committees that have been set up, that there are certain matters which should be taken into consideration when dealing with this great question.
The first is, what attitude is to be taken with regard to civilian health? Last spring I spoke at some length in this house about civilian health. I was prompted to do so by the fact that after the war broke out, it was discovered beyond all question of doubt that the health of the Canadian people, as reflected by the health of the soldiers who had been examined, was just not good, In this connection I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in a recent issue of Health. I enjoy quoting from this publication because I find it invariably hits the nail on the head. This is what they say in the autumn issue with respect to this question:
Soon it will be possible for our authorities to estimate with reasonable accuracy the number of young men in certain age groups who are fit-and by the same token those who are unfit to serve in the army.
Of course in piping times of peace such things are "impossible". One recalls debates in the House of Commons W'hen at the end of interminable talk following a resolution by a 
patriotic medical man to the effect that there should be periodic physical examination of our population the conclusion was reached that the thing was utopian and impossible. And yet shortly with the incentive of war we discover that it is possible and that we have done it.
It is surprising what the Canadian people or the Canadian government can do when faced with such a tragedy as war. The editorial continues:
The percentage of disabilities to be found will doubtless be high. It was high when similar examinations were conducted during the operation of the Military Service Act during the last -war. The revelations made then and about to be made now prove conclusively that from the standpoint of health we constantly neglect large sections of our population.
Thinking people are beginning to wonder what we are going to do about it. Why should we wait until we are faced with a serious war before we begin to take stock of our human assets? Why is the health and welfare of the average young man and woman not an essential objective in peace-time as well as in war-time?
If one desires to ask a further pertinent if not an impertinent question one may enquire why it is that in spite of the increasing disabilities which may be expected from either a financial depression or a war frequently the first thing a government thinks of under such circumstances is to reduce health expenditures instead of increasing them.
That is something that has always been in my mind, and I believe I expressed my feelings when wTe were considering the estimates of the health department. The editorial continues:
When one considers that in war the fit are sacrificed on the altars of Mars and the unfit left at home a situation is discovered which should demand the attention of all political leaders.
Our statesmen on the ivhole have given very little consideration to the subject.
I do trust that these committees and the government will see fit to give proper consideration to the question of health. If we are seriously tackling the problem, the first thing for us to do, because a prerequisite to good health is adequate food, clothing and shelter, is to assure the Canadian people that they shall be provided with the necessities of life so long as we are able to provide them, and if the present financial policy of Canada will not enable the government to do that, there is only one thing for the government to do and that is to change the financial policy.
One thing comes to my mind in that connection. In a recent address the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association is reported to have referred once again to "funny money," and it is significant that he referred to "funny money" on the evening of the same day on which the leader of the Social Credit group spoke in this house.

The Address-Mr. Shaw
I say to the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association that if he wants to talk about "funny money," all he has to do is to talk about his own bankers' money because in the depression we were using the so-called bankers' money, and it must have been "funny money" indeed to bring upon us such conditions as prevailed then during a period of great abundance. So I say that when the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association talks loosely about "funny money" and cautions the government to have nothing to do with it, he is really giving the government a hint to cast him adrift and start building up a financial policy which will provide for the people of Canada those things which are physically possible and desirable.
I wish now to make reference to one question that came up in the last session of parliament, namely the processing tax as it applied to wheat which is gristed in the local mills, where the miller keeps a part of the wheat to pay for the cost of grinding. On August 3 last the question was asked in this house whether the miller would have to pay the processing tax if he took part of the farmer's grain as payment for grinding the balance into flour. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) gave it as his opinion at the time that the miller would have to pay the processing tax. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) then stated that his opinion was that this was no ordinary transaction and therefore he did not think the tax would apply. May I add that the Minister of Trade and Commerce in giving his opinion said that the tax was designed to help the producer.
I have been giving this matter a great deal of consideration especially in view of the fact that the wheat board in its circular of August 16 stated that the processing tax would apply. The farmers take their wheat to the local mills to be ground into flour. How, then, can a processing tax which is charged against that farmer be said to be designed to help the farmer? I have in my constituency at least one privately-owned mill which has been a boon to the farmers of that district for a great many years, and I find upon investigation that the processing tax is a handicap to the farmer. It is an extra charge upon the farmer. How can it be designed to help him if in the final analysis it does him a great deal of harm? So I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, do not leave this matter where it now stands, but let us go into it more fully and when the minister has all the evidence before him I believe he will agree with me that the processing tax should not be applied in the
case of the local mill where the farmer leaves a part of his grain with the miller to pay for the wheat he has had ground into flour.
It was announced during the last session that the processing tax would have to be borne by the miller, and I believe hon. members generally were agreed that that was quite proper. I am speaking from memory but I believe early in August we were advised that the large mills could not stand the 16 cent processing tax. That seems strange, I would Say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not know upon what basis he came to that conclusion or exactly what factors were taken into consideration, but I do know that very soon after the application of the processing tax, which is passed on to the consumer, the large milling companies of this country entered into a price-cutting war and they knocked their prices down and down and down. That is fine for the consumer. Prices went down nearly to where they should be. But it does not substantiate the argument that the large mills were unable to bear the weight of the processing tax.
It is significant, too, that even with the processing tax, and even after it was passed on plus the price war, the five largest milling concerns in Canada recently declared the second highest dividend in five years, a total sum of $2,040,000, approximately, to be distributed in dividends among the shareholders of these concerns.
I have in my constituency near the village of Penhold one of the service flying training schools. I have been given to understand that when sites were being selected for the' establishment of these schools the engineers-were the ones who determined the location and that a field would not be established in a certain constituency just because a Liberal member of parliament happened to reside there. I am satisfied that the practice of having the engineers determine the location is the proper one, and if that is so I would1 Say to the government, for goodness sake send a letter to the defeated candidate in my constituency and to certain newspapers who are building him up for the next election, telling them that it is the engineers who determine the location, for apparently they do not know it. The people of my district are very happy that that school is being established there. We know that it has had a beneficial effect in reducing local unemployment and that it has stimulated business in the vicinity. But I have had disturbing reports about the part being played in the hiring of men by a certain member of the executive of the Edmonton Liberal Association. I am not making any charges and
The Address-Mr. Shaw

therefore I mention no names, but these disturbing reports have come to me from many quarters, and believe me, if it is at all possible I shall run them down.

Thank you, I shall take just
a moment, Mr. Speaker. In the city of Red Deer, in my constituency, we have one of the thirty-day training schools-I know of no better name-and I may say that we are happy to have it there. I had occasion to be in Red Deer on the morning of October 9, when several hundred of these boys detrained at that point, and I was amused to see them march down the avenue; I wondered just how long it would be before they would appear like real soldiers. I happened to be in Red Deer two or three weeks later, and I was particularly pleased to see what grand work had been done in the training of these boys. A good deal of credit is due the officers in charge for their accomplishments. On two occasions I went into the camp. I found among the boys no general resentment at having had to go to camp, but rather they took it like good sports. I had, however, a number of complaints. But I know that the scheme is only in its infancy, and that everything had to be rushed just prior to the opening of the camp. So may I say, Mr. Speaker, this final word, that while I am not lodging any criticism of the camp at the present time, I reserve the right to criticize whenever I believe that criticism is due.
Mr. J. E. S. EMMANUEL D'ANJOU (Rimouski):	(Translation) Mr. Speaker, it
is not without deep emotion that I rise to address the house after an absence of sixteen years. Indeed, I was fortunate enough to be elected in 1917 to represent the electoral division of Rimouski in this house where I sat until 1924. In 1940 the electors of the same county of Rimouski did me the honour of choosing me as their candidate in circumstances almost identical with those of 1917. At that time Canada was at war and conscription was in force. In 1940 Canada is taking part in the war, but, thank God, there is no conscription for overseas service. I came forward as a candidate in Rimouski with the same programme that I had in 1917. I was the candidate of the Liberal party led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and it is as such that I conducted my campaign. I told my electors that
FMr. Shaw.]
I was the official candidate of the King-Lapointe Liberal party. I have come to this house to give my full support to the government in its free and voluntary war effort.
In 1917 I stated to my electors of Rimouski that I was opposed to compulsory military service overseas, and I told them the same thing this year. I declared on many occasions, however, that should circumstances require it I would be the first to shed my blood for the defence of Canada, but that I should refuse to do so outside the country. My views have not changed. I have pledged myself to oppose in this house any move to impose conscription for service overseas, and that promise I will keep. The following words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier represent my views:
Canada first, Canada always, Canada only.
However, when the mobilization act was placed before parliament I did not hesitate to support it.. Section 3 of this act is quite clear:
The powers conferred by the next preceding section may not be exercised for the purpose of requiring persons to serve in the military, naval or air forces outside of Canada and the territorial waters thereof.
My constituents have recognized with me the timeliness of that mobilization act providing solely for the defence in Canada. Those who live in my constituency are justly proud to number among their own people two gallant soldiers, Jean Brillant and Joseph Kable, who, during the last w7ar, had the honour of winning the highest military decoration, the Victoria Cross. How many constituencies in Canada can boast of men to whom such honours have been awarded? I am proud of representing in this house a constituency where national registration has given such splendid results. Every one heeded the call and the registration was complete. Such a wonderful result was largely due to the wise and enlightened directions given by the priests of my constituency, to whom I tender my respectful and sincere thanks. Since the beginning of the session, much has been said about our participation in the war and our war effort but although Canada is at war, we must not overlook the problem of agriculture which is of vital concern to all parts of our dominion. Many hon. members who have preceded me have dealt with agriculture and, I, for one, represent a constituency where agriculture is very progressive, and I should consider myself unfaithful to my duty if I did not deal with this subject to-night. Last year, I requested the Minister of Agriculture to grant, as had been done previously, a sum of S2,500 to the local exhibition in the county of Rimouski.

The Address-Mr. D'Anjou
The grant was refused on account of the heavy expenses which the war entailed. Therefore the exhibition was cancelled. As a rule this exhibition is held in the centre of the county of Rimouski and all the farmers cooperate in sending their various products. Notwithstanding the wide character which the war has assumed, I would request the Minister of Agriculture to grant that amount as he formerly did. He would thus do something useful. While our soldiers are the nation's defenders, the tillers of the soil are not without importance. In order to enable our soldiers to fight, we must feed them and the farmers have to supply them with the necessary foodstuffs. Land is the great provider and it seems to me that without lessening our war effort we should, as far as possible, help the farmers and encourage them as we have done in the past.
Like all those who have preceded me, I must offer my congratulations to the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada for having met the President of the United States and concluded with him an agreement regarding the joint defence of the two countries, since we Canadians are also, after a fashion, Americans. Canada is an American country and it seems to my mind only fair and logical that such an agreement should have been signed. I am convinced that all Canadians, whatever their racial origin, were extremely pleased at the meeting of these two statesmen and heartily approve the agreement arrived at.
I also wish to congratulate and thank the government for having established in Rimouski county a training camp and flying field. I am very grateful to the Minister of National Defence for Air, thanks to whose good offices we were able to obtain these facilities. The establishment of a training camp and flying field in Rimouski county has enormously helped the training of our young men, and has been welcomed by the whole population.
I listened the other night to the excellent speech given in French by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Chambers). In my opinion, the hon. member thereby gave a lesson to a great many members from the province of Quebec who, either through snobbery or for other reasons unknown to me, rarely speak French in this house. When one wishes to preserve a right, it has always been my belief that he must exercise it. Some may consider the matter unimportant; yet I remember an occasion in 1924, the Hon. Mr. Lemieux was speaker at the time, when I arose to make some statement in the house and, turning my eyes towards the clerk's desk, I saw on it a calendar printed in
English only. I then asked the Hon. Mr. Lemieux to be kind enough to give us the bilingual calendar. Two days later we had it. After an absence of sixteen years I returned to the house and, upon entering this chamber, my first impulse was to look at this same calendar to see if it was still bilingual. I am pleased to observe that it is. While visiting the senate chamber the other day, I noticed that their calendar is not bilingual. I trust that some senator from the province of Quebec will be found to request a new one similar to that of the House of Commons.
I also wish to congratulate the government for the excellent appointments it has made in recent weeks. There is always a great deal of eagerness to criticize the government, yet its aceomplishmnts are rarely mentioned. There is nothing like comparison to establish which side has been more beneficial to the country. A close study of the different parties that have held power in Canada and of the various governments which have administered the country since confederation will convince us, and I refer especially to all French-Cana-adians residing in the province of Quebec, that we have enjoyed under Liberal administrations wider recognition of our rights than under Conservative regimes.
Therefore I say that when the government show their willingness to recognize our rights, we should at least have the decency to congratulate them instead of forever criticizing them. As I said, our government have recently made a few commendable appointments. They have appointed Mr. Sirois to the Unemployment Insurance commission. They have appointed Mr. Edmond Cloutier to the position of King's Printer. They have appointed Mr. Leduc to the Supreme Court. And there are many more appointments that I might mention. While admitting that we do not fully enjoy our rights in this country, we should never fail, when the occasion arises, to express our gratitude to the government for whatever they do along that line.
I take this opportunity to congratulate the right hon. the Prime Minister of this country for the splendid speech he delivered the other day and especially for what he said about France. He said that the French-Canadians, and more particularly those who live in the province of Quebec, now have the honour of perpetuating French culture not only in Canada but in the world. On that occasion, the Prime Minister spoke as a great Canadian. But, after all, blood will tell. The right hon. the Prime Minister of this country is the grandson of William Lyon Mackenzie, the patriot who in 1837 fought alongside Papineau for the defence of our most cherished rights. I am sure that French-
The Address-Mr. D'Anjou

Canadians from the province of Quebec and from all Canada will be grateful to the right hon. Prime Minister for the stirring words he spoke on behalf of France. No, Mr. Speaker, France is not dead and will not die. The France of the martyrs, and the missionaries-France, the eldest daughter of the church, cannot die. She will arise, radiant as before. The France who brought to Canada not only the torch of civilization1 but also the cross of Christ, will arise again in all her glory, for, I repeat, France cannot die.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, we French-Canadians are not free from defects. The defects of our qualities, perhaps. As I was just saying, we do not always recognize merit where there is merit. The statesman who is the Prime Minister's chief lieutenant-I refer to the right hon. the Minister of Justice-is the subject of considerable attack, not only in certain sections of Canada but also in the province of Quebec. Political failures unworthy of unloosening his shoe-strings are constantly attacking this man who, as he stated in his radio addresses, is our defender. When congratulating the government on their recent appointments from the French-Cana-dian point of view, I saw in these appointments the hand of the Minister of Justice. Instead of doing justice to our public men while they are living, we always wait till they are dead. To-day we render justice to Chapleau, Mercier and Laurier. I suppose justice will be done to the Minister of Justice after his death. He will occupy a high place in the history of our country. Monuments have been erected to the memory of Laurier and Mercier. Lapointe will have his monument, carved in the granite of the Rocky mountains. That monument will remind our grandchildren and great grandchildren that the Minister of Justice was a great Canadian, a benefactor of his race. If we always kept in mind the motto of the province of Quebec "I remember", we should not forget those who have shed lustre upon our race and who have fought for our rights. I pray the Lord to give long life to the right hon. Minister of Justice, who has inherited Laurier's unblemished mantle, so that he may remain for many years at the helm of our country, not only in the best interests of Canadians of all nationalities, but to ensure that our rights, the rights of French-Canadians of the province of Quebec shall be respected.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I have been happy to do justice to the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada and especially to a man who is denied justice, but whose name shall be written in gold in the history of our country, the right hon. Minister of Justice.
